_comment: Optional example of project-scope permissions, for <project>/.claude/settings.json.
Nothing here is needed to use the skills. It is one person's working setup, kept in its
own file so the line between what this toolkit requires and what someone happens to
prefer stays visible. Take what you want and ignore the rest.
Claude Code merges this on top of ~/.claude/settings.json. The skill scripts and the
read-only git/gh rules stay at user scope and are deliberately NOT repeated here: the
plugin installs once per machine, so its permissions belong at the same scope, and an
allow rule that goes missing costs a prompt and nothing worse.
The ask and deny lists ARE repeated, which is not an oversight. This file is checked in
and the user file is not, so on a clone where nobody merged the user file this is the
whole policy -- and this file grants Read, Edit and Write as tool-level rules. Grant
Read wholesale with no deny block and an agent reads ~/.ssh and your shell history with
nothing in the way. That holds whether or not auto mode is on; auto mode only removes
the prompt that would otherwise have asked. Keep both lists in step with the user file.
defaultMode is absent on purpose. Add "defaultMode": "auto" and the ask list stops
being a second record of a decision and becomes the only thing that asks at all.
env, set, export -p and declare -p are matched EXACTLY, not as prefixes, and printenv is
a prefix rule because its bare form dumps too -- do not 'fix' either to match the other.
The permissions section of the toolkit's README says why.
The deny paths are examples, not a complete set. Add the credential directories and
secret-manager commands your own machine actually has.
A path deny binds the FILE TOOLS -- Read, Edit, Grep -- and not Bash. A blanket
Bash(cat:*) or Bash(grep:*) grant reads ~/.ssh straight past every deny below, and no
Bash deny can fence it: the reader surface is unbounded and a path pattern loses to
cat $HOME/.ssh/id_rsa. So content reads go through Read and Grep, which the denies do
match, and no general-purpose shell reader is granted here. ls, wc, du and tree stay
because they leak metadata rather than contents. find is absent for a second reason:
-delete and -exec make it a write command, and it would pass the Bash(rm:*) ask rule
untouched.
Two example stacks below, Python on uv and TypeScript on pnpm + nx. Delete the half a
project does not use, or both. Dependency installs sit in ask because they change the
tree, which the recommended workflow confirms first.
